This is Tambor de Crioula. 19th century to present.
on_screen: Title card: Tambor de Crioula · Brazil · 19th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated among enslaved African descendants in Maranhão.
The earliest known record dates to 1818, described as a 'batuque.' It was officially registered as Brazilian Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2007.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It is performed for Saint Benedict, birthdays, social gatherings, and celebrations like Carnival or June festivals.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: File:Patrimônio Cultural do Brasil, Tambor de Crioula do Maranhão envolve dança, canto e percussão.webm (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3d/Patrim%C3%B4nio_Cultural_do_Brasil%2C_Tambor_de_Crioula_do_Maranh%C3%A3o_envolve_dan%C3%A7a%2C_canto_e_percuss%C3%A3o.webm?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in a circle.
Women (coreiras) dance individually in the center, inviting others via the 'punga' (a belly-to-belly bump).
Men (coureiros) play drums and lead the singing.
Watch for Punga.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The ensemble consists of three drums (parelhas): the crivador (small), meião (medium), and roncador (large).
Additional instruments include the pandeiro and matracas.
Listen for the crivador, meião, roncador, pandeiro.
A rhythmic, percussive sound dominated by the deep resonance of three handmade drums tuned by fire, accompanied by the sharp clatter of matracas and vibrant, improvisational vocal call-and-response.

Men wear white pants, straw hats, and patterned shirts.
It is performed in squares, terreiros, or at social events.
